news.content_original: Eight more COVID-19 cases in Kolkata amid seasonal surge in viral infections A doctor said the current disease pattern mirrors the Omicron wave, presenting primarily with mild upper respiratory symptoms such as fever, sore throat, cough, and body aches. Written by: Sweety Kumari 3 min read Kolkata Updated: Jul 22, 2026 03:46 PM IST Elderly people and those with comorbidities remain at higher risk of developing severe complications. (File Photo) Eight more people have tested positive for COVID-19 in Kolkata as hospitals report an uptick in cases of coronavirus and influenza amid a seasonal surge in viral infections across West Bengal. Pulmonologists and critical care specialists have reassured the public that the currently circulating pattern is mild. Dr Joydeep Ghosh, Consultant, Internal Medicine, Fortis Hospital, Anandapur, told The Indian Express, “In the last one week I have documented four COVID-19 cases. There are many in the OPD who we know might be positive, but they are not taking the test. The symptoms are the same: high-grade fever and persistent cough. There have been around eight positive cases in our hospital.” Dr Subhajit Sen, Consultant Pulmonologist and Critical Care Specialist at the hospital, gave details of three patients. “One has recovered and been discharged, while two aged between 35 and 65 required ICU admission due to low oxygen levels. Both have responded well to treatment and are now stable, though they have not yet been discharged,” he said. Dr Sen said the current disease pattern mirrors the Omicron wave, presenting primarily with mild upper respiratory symptoms such as fever, sore throat, cough, and body aches. He emphasised, however, that elderly people and those with comorbidities remain at higher risk of developing severe complications. “There is no need to panic, as most patients recover well with timely medical care,” Dr Sen said. “Vigilance, not fear, is the need of the hour.” Dr Sen advised people to take precautions like wearing masks in crowded places, maintaining hand hygiene, avoiding unnecessary gatherings during periods of high transmission, and consulting a doctor promptly if symptoms worsen. Boy with COVID and pneumonia stable A 10-year-old boy from Kolkata ’s Garia neighbourhood had earlier tested positive for COVID-19 and was diagnosed with pneumonia. The boy, who presented with fever, cold, and respiratory distress, was taken to Peerless Hospital on Saturday. Following a comprehensive viral panel test, doctors confirmed COVID-19 infection and detected signs of pneumonia on his chest X-ray. Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads. The boy is receiving treatment in the hospital’s Pediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU). Hospital officials confirmed that his condition remains stable. Also Read | 10-year-old boy tests positive for Covid-19 in Kolkata As a precautionary measure, the boy’s mother has been placed in isolation, and COVID-19 tests have been initiated for other family members. Hospital officials stated that routine panel testing often picks up mild cases that might otherwise go undiagnosed. “Every two to three months, we see isolated COVID-19 cases, but they are overwhelmingly mild,” a hospital representative said. Medical experts have advised parents that while viral fevers and coughs are common among children during the monsoon season, cases involving prolonged fever or breathing difficulty should be evaluated by a physician promptly. © The Indian Express Pvt Ltd Sweety Kumari Sweety Kumari is a seasoned journalist reporting from West Bengal for The Indian Express. news.title: Anthony Fauci to testify about COVID-19 pandemic at Senate hearing
news.excerpt: Anthony Fauci, who led the government's response to COVID-19, will testify at a Senate hearing after Sen. Rand Paul accused him of destroying records.
news.rss_summary_html: Anthony Fauci, who led the government's response to COVID-19, will testify at a Senate hearing after Sen. Rand Paul accused him of destroying records.

news.content_title: Anthony Fauci to testify about COVID-19 pandemic at Senate hearing
news.content: POLITICS Anthony Fauci Anthony Fauci to testify about COVID-19 pandemic at Senate hearing Paul has investigated for years whether COVID-19 leaked from a Chinese lab. But Fauci previously testified that he believes the most likely origin was from animal-to-human transmission. Bart Jansen USA TODAY Updated July 23, 2026, 2:15 p.m. ET WASHINGTON – Anthony Fauci, the former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases who has been criticized by many Republican lawmakers for his response to the COVID-19 pandemic, will testify July 29 at a Senate committee . Sen. Rand Paul, R-Kentucky, who arranged for the hearing, accused Fauci of destroying government records after directing the pandemic. Some lawmakers have also questioned Fauci’s recommendations for social distancing to prevent the spread of the virus. Paul, who heads the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, has jousted with Fauci for years about whether the U.S. government funded research at the Chinese lab that may have developed the coronavirus that sparked the worldwide pandemic in 2020. But Fauci has strongly denied in previous congressional testimony the allegations that he tried to cover up the theory that COVID-19 leaked from the Wuhan Institute of Virology in China. The U.S. intelligence community has assessed that the virus wasn't developed as a biological weapon and that China had no advance warning of it. But the intelligence community couldn't determine whether the virus was genetically engineered. Part of the dispute is about coronavirus research into how disease jumps from one species to another, which is called “gain of function” research. The Defense Department pursued such research two years before the pandemic. Ralph Baric, a coronavirus researcher, told the committee he never “ruled out a lab-leak possibility.” Paul said Fauci condemned and demeaned anyone who argued that the pandemic could have leaked from the lab and never accepted responsibility for funding dangerous research. “At next week’s hearing, I will make sure Fauci answers for his dangerous decisions and the consequences they had for millions,” Paul said on social media . But Fauci, who retired in 2022 after 54 years at the institute, told a House committee in June 2024 that he never influenced research on the origins of the virus. He said then that he believed the most likely origin was from animal-to-human transmission. "I've also been very, very clear, and said multiple times, that I don’t think the concept of there being a lab (leak) is inherently a conspiracy theory," Fauci said. "What is conspiracy is the kind of distortions of that particular subject, like it was a lab leak, and I was parachuted into the CIA like Jason Bourne and told the CIA that they should really not be talking about a lab leak.” Witnesses including a former Fauci aide, David Morens, have told lawmakers that they deleted correspondence and used private emails to get around public records laws. But Fauci denied ever using a private email address to discuss government business and he downplayed how closely he worked with Morens and said their offices were in different buildings. Fauci also described harassment and death threats he and his family received after being vilified by many Republican lawmakers over his pandemic stances and championing of COVID vaccines. Contributing: Reuters Featured Weekly Ad

Fauci has denied these accusations, maintaining his belief in animal-to-human transmission as the most likely origin and refuting claims of covering up the lab-leak theory. The hearing follows years of disputes between Fauci and Paul over U.S. funding of research at a Chinese lab and Fauci's recommendations for social distancing. Fauci has also reported receiving harassment and death threats.

elements_en.event: Anthony Fauci, former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, will testify at a Senate committee hearing on July 29, 2026, regarding his response to the COVID-19 pandemic. The hearing was arranged by Senator Rand Paul, R-Kentucky, who has accused Fauci of destroying government records and questioned his recommendations for social distancing.
elements_en.scale_impact_and_risk: No specific case counts, deaths, or exposures reported. The hearing focuses on Fauci's pandemic response decisions, including his stance on the origins of COVID-19 (animal-to-human transmission vs. lab leak) and his handling of government records. Risk level not explicitly stated.
elements_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: Fauci has denied allegations of covering up the lab-leak theory, destroying records, or using private emails for government business. He maintains that the most likely origin of COVID-19 was animal-to-human transmission. The hearing aims to hold Fauci accountable for his pandemic decisions. Fauci has also reported harassment and death threats. The intelligence community assessed the virus was not a biological weapon but could not determine if it was genetically engineered.

news.content_title: Exclusive | Pentagon asked for 'gain of function' research proposals years before COVID-19 pandemic, top virologist tells Congress
news.content: See more of our coverage in your search results. WASHINGTON — A War Department program requested proposals for so-called “gain of function” experiments that could make viruses more infectious nearly two full years before the COVID-19 pandemic began, a top US virologist told Congress earlier this year. Dr. Ralph Baric, a prominent coronavirus researcher, told the Senate Homeland Security Committee in a closed-door interview April 10 that the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) had solicited proposals in January 2018 to understand “what drives cross-species jumping” in viruses. “Now, if you want to know, down to the nucleotide level, what drives a cross-species jumping event, you are talking gain-of-function experiments,” Baric told committee staffers, according to an interview transcript obtained by The Post. 6 WASHINGTON — A Defense Department program requested research proposals years before the COVID-19 pandemic for so-called “gain of function” experiments that could make viruses more infectious, according to Dr. Ralph Baric. UNC GILLINGS SCHOOL OF GLOBAL PUBLIC HEALTH Senate Homeland Security Committee Chairman Rand Paul (R-Paul.) is making Baric’s full testimony available at a Reading Room webpage that is dedicated to providing Americans full transparency about the decisions surrounding viral research leading up to the global outbreak. US public health officials like former National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Disease (NIAID) Director Dr. Anthony Fauci have maintained that the research — which can involve the enhancement of potential pandemic pathogens — is safe and useful for developing vaccines or other drugs to fight emerging viruses. Critics have argued that there are no civilian applications for what they deem risky viral research — and that one of the proposals DARPA received included identical characteristics to SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19. That proposal, known as Project DEFUSE, has since been cited by scientists as “smoking gun” evidence that COVID-19 was engineered in a Wuhan, China lab because the same furin cleavage site later discovered in the virus itself. It had been submitted by Baric; Shi Zhengli, a top scientist working with bat coronaviruses at the now-infamous Wuhan Institute of Virology (WIV); and Dr. Peter Daszak, the president of since-debarred nonprofit EcoHealth Alliance that took millions of dollars in federal grants to fund research meant to prevent pandemics. “We’ve never dropped a furin cleavage site into a coronavirus like that,” Baric acknowledged in his Senate interview, adding that he “hadn’t remembered the grant” from 2018 even as he and other scientists were furiously debating the origins of COVID in early 2020. The draft proposal was first made public by The Intercept in 2021. Daszak wrote that he would “downplay” the involvement of Chinese researchers when asking for federal funding, according to drafts also published by US Right To Know. 6 US public health officials like former National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Disease Director Dr. Anthony Fauci have maintained that the research is safe and useful for developing vaccines or other drugs to fight emerging viruses. Getty Images DARPA asked for the research plans through its Preventing Emerging Pathogenic Threats (PREEMPT) program in order to study at least 15 pathogens that could infect US troops abroad, said Baric, adding the experiments were supposed to be conducted in a “controlled” laboratory setting. When questioned by committee chief counsel Christina Salazar about who was supposed to perform the actual gain-of-function experiment on the resulting virus, Baric responded, “That part would be done by me.” 6 Critics have argued that there are no civilian applications for what they deem risky viral research. AFP via Getty Images “Do you think that Dr. Shi and WIV had the technical capability of doing the work proposed in DEFUSE on their own?” Salazar also asked. “Absolutely,” Baric responded. 6 “Dr. Fauci and his virologist allies privately believed that the pandemic may have come from a lab leak but publicly argued that a lab leak was implausible,” Paul said in a statement. REUTERS Ultimately, Project DEFUSE was never funded. However, former Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Director Dr. Robert Redfield noted during an October 2024 biosecurity panel that even unfunded projects and proposals can be tested under other research grants. “Research grants are always written in the context of being more fluid than contracts,” Baric confirmed in his testimony, adding that due to sub-standard lab conditions, “you cannot ever conclusively say that there was not a laboratory leak” that started the pandemic, though he claimed that a natural origin was still the “most likely” theory. 6 DARPA asked for the research plans through its PREEMPT program to study at least 15 pathogens that could infect US troops abroad and the experiments were supposed to be conducted in a “controlled” laboratory setting, Baric noted. Getty Images “I never ruled out lab leak possibility,” Baric said. “I don’t see how anyone can. And the reason that is, is that they’ve published papers saying that they did their work at BSL-2. Biological Safety Level 2 is less stringent than Biological Safety Level 3. So there are many more laboratory-acquired infections at BSL-2 than at BSL-3.” Baric also shared details from private meetings in January 2020 and February 2020 that showed Fauci and other top US scientists debated whether gain-of-function research could have started the pandemic — despite the then-NIAID head’s repeated denials to Congress of that possibility in subsequent years. 6 The proposal, known as Project DEFUSE, has since been cited by scientists as “smoking gun” evidence that COVID-19 was engineered in a Wuhan lab because the same furin cleavage site later discovered in the virus itself. REUTERS Those meetings included phone calls with scientists whom Fauci later prompted to write a paper debunking the lab leak theory. In a previously undisclosed interaction, Fauci also took interest in a paper that Baric had authored that stemmed from NIH-funded research that involved “potential gain-of-function related experiments,” the latter testified. Fauci “got called away for a phone call in a SCIF [Secure Compartmented Information Facility], and so he left pretty early in the meeting,” claimed Baric, adding that the other National Institutes of Health officials couldn’t locate documents associated with the study, titled, “A SARS-like cluster of circulating bat coronaviruses shows potential for human emergence.” At least “90%” of the research for that paper was completed before the Obama administration instituted a pause on all gain-of-function research, Baric said, but some of the work that Shi performed at WIV wasn’t acknowledged — at the behest of Daszak — until five years after it was published in 2015. “Is it something that typically happens five years later?” Salazar asked Baric. “Not typically, but it does happen,” he replied. EcoHealth Alliance, now disbanded, was barred from receiving US funding until 2030 for not providing evidence that its research abided by the Obama-era gain-of-function pause and submitted to timely reviews as required. Paul will have the opportunity to ask Fauci about Baric’s testimony during a public committee hearing July 29, as well as findings from the senator’s investigation that he claims show the ex-White House COVID czar “destroyed government records and recommended that other members of government delete emails and then delete them from their deleted files.” “Dr. Fauci and his virologist allies privately believed that the pandemic may have come from a lab leak but publicly argued that a lab leak was implausible,” Paul said in a statement. “They conspired to condemn and demean anyone who argued that the pandemic could have leaked from the Wuhan Lab and never, ever accepted responsibility for the terrible decision to fund this dangerous research in China.” A former senior adviser to Fauci, Dr. David Morens, was indicted in April for concealing and destroying records critical to uncovering the origins of COVID-19

analysis.brief_en: A top US virologist revealed that the Pentagon requested 'gain of function' research proposals years before the COVID-19 pandemic, according to Senate testimony. Dr. Ralph Baric confirmed that DARPA solicited proposals in January 2018 to study cross-species virus jumping, which he acknowledged required gain-of-function experiments. The proposal, known as Project DEFUSE, included characteristics matching SARS-CoV-2 but was never funded. Baric stated he couldn't rule out a lab leak possibility due to sub-standard lab conditions, though he maintained a natural origin was most likely. The testimony revealed private debates among US scientists about whether gain-of-function research could have triggered the pandemic, contradicting public statements.

news.content: New Covid variants BA.2.86, RF.5: Symptoms, risks and precautions Experts urge that there is no need to panic, but staying sensible is important By: Lifestyle Desk 4 min read New Delhi Jul 23, 2026 02:00 PM IST Here's what you should consider (Photo: Getty Images/Thinkstock) Amid reports of an uptick in cases in Andhra Pradesh, we asked experts about how BA.2.86 and RF.5 — newer sub-variants of the Omicron variant of Covid-19 — are different and precautionary steps to take. Dr Rituja Ugalmugle, consultant, internal medicine, Wockhardt Hospitals, Mumbai Central, said that these have accumulated more genetic changes over time. Like previous Omicron variants, they mainly cause upper respiratory symptoms and usually lead to milder illness in people who have immunity from vaccination or past infections. Dr Ugalmugle said BA.2.86 is also known as ‘Pirola’, and is a heavily mutated strain that first emerged in mid-2023. DISCLAIMER: This article is based on information from the public domain and/or the experts we spoke to. Always consult your health practitioner before starting any routine. “What makes them different is their ability to spread easily and partially escape immunity, which is why they are still being watched. Currently, there is no strong evidence showing that these variants consistently cause more severe illness than the earlier Omicron strains, but they can still be a serious risk for older adults, pregnant women, people with chronic illnesses, and those with weakened immune systems,” said Dr Ugalmugle. While both belong to the Omicron family, which is known for spreading easily, they differ slightly in their genetic makeup. “BA.2 is a well-known Omicron subvariant, while RF.5 is a recombinant variant, meaning it is formed when two different Omicron subvariants exchange genetic material during infection. Both variants mainly spread through respiratory droplets and close contact,” said Dr Harish Chafle, senior consultant, chest physician, bronchoscopist, intensivist and sleep disorders specialist, Gleneagles Hospitals Parel Mumbai. “At present, there is no clear evidence that RF.5 causes more severe illness than BA.2. However, recombinant variants are closely monitored because they may spread differently or partially evade immunity,” added Dr Chafle. Story continues below this ad Are there any symptoms people should watch out for? The symptoms are mostly similar to those seen with other recent Covid-19 variants. The most commonly reported symptoms include fever, sore throat, cough, nasal congestion, fatigue, headache, and body aches. “Some people might also have a hoarse voice or mild gastrointestinal issues like nausea or diarrhoea. Since these symptoms can overlap with flu and other viral infections during the monsoon, testing becomes important, especially for those at higher risk or with ongoing or worsening symptoms. Breathlessness, chest pain, confusion, or a drop in oxygen levels should always be taken seriously and need immediate medical care,” said Dr Ugalmugle. Ensure you follow hand hygiene (Photo: AI Generated) What precautions should people take, and is there any reason to panic? There is no need to panic, but staying sensible is important. According to Dr Ugalmugle, Covid-19 has become a recurring viral illness, and new variants will likely drive periodic waves. The precautions are familiar and effective: stay home if you feel unwell, practice good hand hygiene, wear a mask in crowded indoor spaces if you are vulnerable or showing symptoms, and keep vaccinations or booster shots up to date if recommended. “People with diabetes, heart disease, lung disease, kidney disease, or weakened immunity should seek medical advice early if they develop symptoms instead of waiting for their condition to worsen. The goal is not to fear every new variant but to respond with awareness, get tested when necessary, and seek appropriate medical care,” said Dr Ugalmugle. (WLBT) - Nearly 3,000 bus drivers, educators and police officers attended the Rankin County School District’s first in-person convocation since the COVID-19 pandemic.The event focused on strategies for creating a safer environment for students and faculty. The keynote speaker was Max Schachter, a national school safety advocate whose son was killed in the 2018 Parkland, Florida school shooting.Keynote speaker calls for legislative actionSchachter said his message centers on teaching others how to prevent tragedies at schools across the country.“What I’m trying to do is get legislators to increase funding for school safety in Mississippi — they haven’t put in a school safety bill in a long time,” Schachter said. “So I would ask for the legislators to look at what Florida is doing and adopt some of the school safety bills.”Schachter also recognized Rankin County School District Superintendent Shane Sanders, noting that Sanders visited the Parkland campus following the 2018 shooting.“I appreciate Rankin and the superintendent Shane Sanders for being such a great leader,” Schachter said. “He came to Parkland after the tragedy and walked through the site of the shooting, and he took a lot of the lessons, learned to make sure it doesn’t happen again.”Superintendent, educators reflect on the eventSanders said Schachter’s presence made the convocation more meaningful.“A dad who lost a child in that tragedy, who has dedicated his life and work to helping others learn through that — that’s pretty powerful to me,” Sanders said.Melody Macon, a 26-year educator who was named Rankin County School District Teacher of the Year, said student safety depends on a community-wide effort.“They’ve added an extra seal on our windows that are bulletproof, and I know Rankin County is doing everything they can to keep us safe, but I just want it to continue,” Macon said.Educators told 3 On Your Side they left the building with new tools, a new sense of purpose and a shared goal: making safety more than a policy - but a promise. analysis.brief_en: The Rankin County School District in Mississippi held its first in-person convocation since the COVID-19 pandemic on July 24, 2026, with nearly 3,000 bus drivers, educators, and police officers attending. The event, reported by WLBT, centered on strategies for enhancing school safety, featuring keynote speaker Max Schachter, a national school safety advocate whose son was killed in the 2018 Parkland shooting. Schachter called for legislative action to increase school safety funding in Mississippi, drawing lessons from Florida's policies. Superintendent Shane Sanders and educators emphasized the importance of community-wide efforts, noting new safety measures like bulletproof window seals. Participants left with renewed purpose to make safety a priority beyond policy.

Newly released Slack messages show an author assigned a 30% probability to a lab origin of the disease By Louis Casiano Fox News Published July 21, 2026 7:00pm EDT Facebook Twitter Threads Flipboard Comments Print Email Add Fox News on Google close Video Biden’s FBI reportedly blocked questioning of COVID-19 researcher New documents reveal the FBI blocked Customs and Border Protection from questioning former President of EcoHealth Alliance Peter Daszak, a researcher linked to the Wuhan Institute of Virology and gain-of-function research. Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., and GOP lawmakers criticized the Biden administration's actions regarding the COVID-19 origins investigation. NEWYou can now listen to Fox News articles! Newly released messages among the authors of a widely cited paper regarding the origins of COVID-19 privately raised doubts that the virus originated from bats, as their paper stated. Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., on Tuesday released the internal Slack messages exchanged among the authors of "The Proximal Origin of SARS-CoV-2" — Kristian Andersen, Robert Garry, Eddie Holmes and Andrew Rambaut."The idea that it came from a lab is implausible, and, yet, privately they're saying the opposite. ... This level of dishonesty, I think, needs to be exposed," Paul told Fox News. "These are people who get large, multimillion-dollar grants from our country, and we shouldn't be giving money to people who lied to us." The paper was published in Nature Medicine in March 2020 and was widely cited by public health officials and the media as the scientific authority for ruling out a laboratory origin of SARS-CoV-2. However, the released messages appear to show that its authors were less certain than their public conclusions suggested. LEGACY MEDIA IGNORES MASSIVE ANTHONY FAUCI DOCUMENT RELEASE ALLEGING HE MISLED CONGRESS ON COVID ORIGINS Video Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., on Tuesday released the internal Slack messages exchanged among the authors of "The Proximal Origin of SARS-CoV-2." (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc, File) Some raised concerns that the virus originated in a lab. Andersen assigned a 30% probability to a lab origin, while Holmes gave an estimate of 20%, though he later revised that to 10%. Either way, both figures contrast with the paper's public assertion that the virus had not been manipulated. "The part I’m really struggling with is that, at the end of the day, we really don’t have any hard evidence one way or the other — and especially given some of the recent evidence, we also can’t rule out that somebody actually put it in there," Andersen wrote on June 11, 2020, according to the documents. "That’s obviously not to say that somebody did, but we can’t rule it out. Our paper was pretty strong in saying ‘there’s no way,’ but I have less confidence in that statement at this stage." RAND PAUL BRINGS CIA WHISTLEBLOWER TO SENATE HEARING ALLEGING 'DEEP STATE' COVID-19 CONSPIRACY The P4 laboratory, center, on the campus of the Wuhan Institute of Virology in China. The lab has been at the center of alleged theories that COVID-19 was engineered in a lab. (Hector Retamal/AFP via Getty Images, File) The documents also reveal internal debates over the furin cleavage site, the genetic feature at the heart of the lab-leak question. At one point, Andersen told colleagues that "some smoking(ish) guns" had emerged that made him "not comfortable" and that he had "less confidence ... at this stage," a news release from Paul's office states.In addition, the authors coordinated with the U.S. intelligence community and National Institutes of Health (NIH) leadership as they were publicly defending their conclusions. Another topic of discussion among the authors was Ralph Baric, a prominent coronavirus researcher.While they acknowledged his expertise, their internal messages revealed a highly contentious relationship with him, characterized by professional rivalry and suspicions that he actively tried to undermine them. GABBARD SPOTLIGHTS FAUCI, COVID-ORIGIN QUESTIONS IN FINAL ACT AS INTELLIGENCE CHIEF AMID SUCCESSION FIGHT Officials with U.S. Customs and Border Protection were allegedly prepared to question and search Peter Daszak, inset, upon his return to the U.S. from the World Health Organization’s investigation into the origins of COVID-19, before the FBI intervened and asked agents to stand down, according to documents released Monday by Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky. (Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs; Getty Images, File)They also suspected Baric was the anonymous leaker, whom they dubbed "Deep Throat," who shared confidential peer-review information with a journalist. The leak suggested that the authors initially suspected a lab origin before changing their minds.A World Health Organization (WHO) scientific advisory group released a report last year on the origins of COVID-19, concluding that the deadly pandemic was caused by "zoonotic spillover," either directly from bats or through an intermediate host. On Monday, Paul released documents that revealed U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agents were preparing to question British zoologist Peter Daszak upon his return to the United States from the World Health Organization’s investigation into the origins of COVID-19, before the FBI intervened and asked agents to stand down. Video Dr. Anthony Fauci, the face of the U.S. response to the pandemic, is slated to testify before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on the origins of the virus this month after a subpoena was issued by Paul, the committee chairperson.CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fauci has been accused by some of manipulating intelligence on the origins of the pandemic and lying to Congress to cover up alleged wrongdoing. Businesses to Risky SuitsJuly 21, 2026, 9:00 AM UTC James Matheson ReporterImpending deadlines are driving business owners to litigate denied and delayed Covid-19 tax credits, despite warnings from attorneys that the unsettled legal landscape makes winning uncertain and expensive.Since the Employee Retention Credit’s creation in 2020, tax lawyers have advised clients to wait rather than rush into lawsuits, since early plaintiffs would bear the costs of governmental opposition, underdeveloped case law, and litigation fees that could outweigh any refund.For those not yet ready to sue, a newer administrative option may offer some breathing room. But six years later — with a looming two-year statute of limitations to contest ERC disallowances — taxpayers are running out of patience to watch for positive results in other cases, leading to a wave of new suits, according to Edward Zollars, a CPA at Thomas, Zollars & Lynch Ltd.“We’re about out of time to wait for somebody to go first, so now we’re just seeing a flood of these,” Zollars said. “They’re coming in either because they got tired of waiting — and they’ve been waiting quite a while — or they have a denial and the two-year clock’s running.”Helping Small Businesses?The ERC was designed to help small- and medium-sized businesses keep employees on payroll, but thousands of businesses still haven’t received the promised tax relief and are turning to court to collect.Created under the first major Covid-19 stimulus law, the ERC can be used by businesses against applicable employment taxes. To qualify, business operations must have been fully or partially suspended due to a Covid-19 government order, or the business must have experienced a significant decline in gross receipts.The government issued its first batch of 28,000 ERC denial letters in July and August 2024, so closure of the two-year statute of limitations is approaching. Roughly 20,000 outstanding ERC claims are still being processed, an IRS report said.Meanwhile, federal courts are increasingly upholding IRS refund rejections, citing insufficient connection between business disruptions and official government orders.Tom Cullinan, a shareholder and ERC practice member at Chamberlain Hrdlicka Law, said the reluctance among tax experts to immediately litigate caused a long delay in substantive ERC cases reaching a courtroom. While taxpayers could have sued six months after filing refund claims, few wanted to take that risk, opting to wait for someone else to shoulder the cost and burden of being the pioneer litigant, he said.As a result, many early ERC refund cases have been “skeletal in their claim,” providing a lackluster coupling of business impact and government orders in effect during the quarters when businesses would claim refunds, Zollars said.“We need people to take real claims with real facts and give us a definition of what the heck is a partial suspension, and what exactly does it mean for a government order to lead to that,” Zollars said. “These are the first ones we’re seeing.”As the legal landscape evolves, several recent cases have started shaping what defines eligibility. In Tri-State Memorial Hospital v. United States, a federal judge rejected the argument that a nonprofit hospital must allege ceasing a significant portion of operations to be eligible, accepting its “but for” a specific gubernatorial order standard. But the US Court of Federal Claims took the opposite position in Northeast Health Services, LLC v. United States, adopting a more stringent standard, holding that a business must show the government order was the proximate cause of a shutdown.Simultaneously, a California federal court denied a construction company’s $1 million refund for failing to directly link its claim to an official shutdown order, while a Mississippi court held in two cases that separate businesses adequately alleged Covid-19 shutdown orders caused a partial suspension of business operations and didn’t need to identify specific orders at the pleading stage. “You’re starting to see more and more of these businesses willing to go to court and bearing the expense,” Cullinan said. “You’re going to start seeing, unfortunately, more and more cases in court.”Litigation AlternativeDespite the two-year lawsuit filing deadline, tax practitioners still advise ERC claimants to wait and see because a litigation alternative exists. Introduced in April 2026, Form 907 agreements extend the review period for disallowed refunds; taxpayers qualify if they have six months or less remaining on their two-year deadline and are waiting for an IRS response to their disallowance protest.Guinevere Moore, managing member of Moore Tax Law Group, recommends filing a Form 907 because as case law develops, taxpayers will be better positioned to negotiate settlements — provided the law moves in their favor.“Someone has to be first,” Moore said. “There’s a very well-known adage, ‘bad facts make bad law.’ I hope that courts are fearful to not make sweeping statements.”Moore noted courts and the IRS are interpreting ERC eligibility too narrowly by treating the credit as assuming taxpayers fall outside its scope, leading to an overly restrictive view of what qualifies as a partial suspension.“I am incredibly disappointed in the way the Internal Revenue Service has been administering the credit,” Moore said. “This credit was intended to be broad-reaching, emergency relief provided to businesses that were made a promise.”Cullinan called the IRS and Justice Department thorough but fair adversaries, noting the DOJ has successfully resolved a large number of cases rather than yielding to a high volume of unfounded claims. Even so, he acknowledged clients who are unable to file an extension and awaiting IRS action present a difficult counseling challenge.“It puts us in a weird position because we’ve routinely told clients, ‘Wait, wait, wait on the IRS; court should be your last choice,’” Cullinan said. “Patience really is wearing out.” Continue Reading Learn more about Bloomberg Tax or Log In to keep reading: See Breaking News in Context From research to software to news, find what you need to stay ahead. Even so, he acknowledged clients who are unable to file an extension and awaiting IRS action present a difficult counseling challenge.“It puts us in a weird position because we’ve routinely told clients, ‘Wait, wait, wait on the IRS; court should be your last choice,’” Cullinan said. “Patience really is wearing out.” Continue Reading Learn more about Bloomberg Tax or Log In to keep reading: See Breaking News in Context From research to software to news, find what you need to stay ahead. analysis.time: Publication date: July 21, 2026. Event timeframe: Ongoing litigation wave approaching two-year statute of limitations deadline for contesting Employee Retention Credit (ERC) disallowances.
analysis.location_and_population: Affected population: Small- and medium-sized businesses that applied for ERC tax credits but received denials or delays.
analysis.event: Businesses are filing lawsuits against the IRS to collect denied or delayed Covid-19 Employee Retention Credits due to approaching two-year statute of limitations deadlines. Tax lawyers previously advised waiting for case law development, but patience is waning.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Thousands of businesses affected; 28,000 denial letters issued in July-August 2024; roughly 20,000 ERC claims still processing. Risk: High litigation costs and uncertain outcomes due to unsettled legal standards on eligibility criteria.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Federal courts are increasingly upholding IRS rejections, citing insufficient links between business disruptions and government orders. Legal standards remain inconsistent across jurisdictions, with cases defining eligibility for partial suspension and government order causation. No official resolution or guidance provided.

analysis.brief_en: As the two-year statute of limitations approaches for contesting denied Employee Retention Credits (ERC), thousands of small- and medium-sized businesses in the U.S. are filing lawsuits against the IRS. The ERC, created under the first major Covid-19 stimulus law, was designed to help businesses retain employees, but thousands still await promised relief. Federal courts are increasingly upholding IRS rejections, citing insufficient connections between business disruptions and government orders, creating inconsistent legal standards. With roughly 20,000 ERC claims still processing and high litigation costs, businesses face uncertain outcomes in their pursuit of refunds.

analysis.brief_en: West Virginia launched an initiative to attract digital nomads by offering financial incentives during the COVID-19 pandemic. The program aimed to boost the state's economy and population by remote workers. According to reports, many of these nomads have decided to remain in West Virginia beyond the initial pandemic period, indicating a successful retention strategy. The state's approach highlights innovative economic recovery efforts during the global health crisis.

According to reports, many of these nomads have decided to remain in West Virginia beyond the initial pandemic period, indicating a successful retention strategy. The state's approach highlights innovative economic recovery efforts during the global health crisis.

Scenario-Based Modeling Study 【字体: 大 中 小 】 时间:2026年07月23日 来源:International Journal of Infectious Diseases 4.6 编辑推荐: 背景COVID-19大流行突显了及时公共卫生干预措施对流行病控制的重要性。韩国实施了疫苗接种、检测、接触者追踪和社交距离以限制传播。本研究评估了这些措施的影响,以为大流行防范提供信息。方法研究人员利用监测数据校准了一个年龄特异性V-SEIQR模型,该模型纳入疫 Research article Open access 背景COVID-19大流行突显了及时公共卫生干预措施对流行病控制的重要性。韩国实施了疫苗接种、检测、接触者追踪和社交距离以限制传播。本研究评估了这些措施的影响,以为大流行防范提供信息。方法研究人员利用监测数据校准了一个年龄特异性V-SEIQR模型,该模型纳入疫苗接种计数、Q-proportion(确诊病例在诊断时已处于隔离状态的占比,用作接触者追踪表现的代理指标)、检测能力和社交距离强度。基于情景的分析比较了前Delta时期(2020年11月1日至2021年6月30日)和Delta时期(2021年7月1日至2021年12月31日)期间替代性政策的时间安排和强度,以累计确诊病例为主要结局。结果将疫苗接种提前两个月可使确诊病例减少48%,表明更早部署比更快接种速度影响更大。检测能力降低会增加疫情负担。较低的Q-proportion与更大的病例负担相关。在Delta时期,推迟“逐步恢复新常态”政策或维持更长时间更严格的社交距离可缓解疫情反弹。结论更早的疫苗部署、持续的检测和接触者追踪能力以及及时的社交距离调整对疫情动态至关重要。在统一建模框架内量化这些效应,为支持大流行防范规划提供了结构化、政策特定的证据。 **论文解读:韩国COVID-19控制政策反事实评估的情景建模研究****研究背景与现存问题** COVID-19大流行对全球公共卫生体系构成严峻挑战,尤其在缺乏有效疫苗或治疗手段的初期,非药物干预措施(NPIs)如检测、接触者追踪、隔离、检疫和社交距离成为控制传播的关键。韩国在2015年中东呼吸综合征(MERS)疫情经验基础上,迅速建立了诊断检测系统、流行病学调查框架和实时监测体系,并实施严格检疫协议,在没有全国封锁的情况下有效控制了病毒传播。2021年初疫苗引入后,优先覆盖高风险人群和医护人员,但过早放松NPIs可能导致疫情反弹。因此,制定兼顾疫苗部署和持续实施NPIs的循证策略至关重要。 然而,评估国家疫情应对效果面临方法论挑战,尤其是缺乏统一评价标准。已有研究多采用描述性趋势分析、统计模型或复合指数(如牛津COVID-19政府响应追踪器),但这些方法难以充分反映干预措施在实际动态环境中的多因素交互效应。为克服这些局限,数学建模提供了一种结构化框架,可模拟疾病传播并评估假设条件下的干预情景,使政策制定者能够探索“假设”情景并评估潜在结果。韩国此前已有建模研究评估社交距离、检测、接触者追踪和疫苗接种的效果,但模型精度常受限于参数假设,需通过实证校准。随着疫情应对证据库的积累,开发适应性且基于实证的评估框架对指导未来公共卫生准备日益重要。 **研究目的** 本研究旨在回顾性评估韩国在Delta变异株出现前后两个时期(前Delta期:2020年11月–2021年6月;Delta主导期:2021年7月–2021年12月),疫苗接种、诊断检测、接触者追踪和社交距离措施如何影响COVID-19传播。通过使用确定性分室模型,研究人员在统一框架内评估了政策特定的反事实情景,并检验替代策略是否可能更有效地缓解传播。 **主要关键技术方法** 研究人员采用韩国疾病控制与预防机构(KDCA)和韩国统计局的公开数据,包括每日新增确诊病例(按年龄组)、疫苗接种计数(按年龄和疫苗类型)、新确诊者中诊断时已隔离的比例(Q-proportion,作为接触者追踪表现的代理指标)以及Delta变异株占比。研究开发了一个年龄结构化的确定性V-SEIQR分室模型,将人群分为三个年龄组(0–19岁、20–64岁、65岁及以上),并模拟两种毒株(前Delta变异株和Delta变异株)。模型通过易感(S)、暴露(E)、感染(I)、隔离(Q)和移除(R)分室描述疾病进展,并纳入疫苗接种状态和免疫力衰减。时间变化输入包括每日疫苗接种计数和每周Q-proportion。传播动力学由有效接触率(β)和Delta变异株相对传播性(φ)驱动,通过局部随机搜索程序校准,以拟合观察到的确诊病例。政策情景设计涵盖四个维度:疫苗接种(部署时间和接种速度)、检测能力(通过检测率参数降低模拟)、接触者追踪(通过Q-proportion变化模拟)和社交距离(通过调整β模拟)。数据来源为韩国国家监测数据,无具体样本队列,但使用了公开汇总数据。 **研究结果** **前Delta期政策效果评估** 在前Delta期,疫苗覆盖率有限,控制策略主要依赖NPIs。通过情景分析,研究人员发现: - **疫苗接种情景**:提前两个月部署疫苗可使累计确诊病例减少48%(情景4),而延迟两个月则增加14%(情景2)。表明更早部署比更快接种速度影响更大。 - **检测能力情景**:检测能力降至参考水平的97.5%或95%时,病例轨迹在12月高峰后开始上升;降至90%时,病例从3月起快速偏离。 - **接触者追踪情景**:将Q-proportion提高10%或维持在50%可减少约65%的累计确诊病例;而降低至95%则导致病例增加1.9倍。 - **社交距离情景**:在11月病例激增期间加强社交距离强度可有效降低传播,最严格的情景(情景3)使流行曲线明显趋平。 **Delta主导期政策效果评估** Delta时期疫苗快速推进,同时围绕放松社交距离的政策讨论持续。情景分析显示: - **疫苗接种速度情景**:将接种速度提高2.5倍可减少约20%的累计确诊病例并降低Delta暴发峰值;而速度减慢至80%时差异不大。 - **检测能力情景**:若仅检测97.5%的感染,累计病例增加约1.5倍,峰值超过10,000例;若仅检测90%,病例增加4.7倍。 - **接触者追踪情景**:维持Q-proportion在45%可减少74%的病例;提高10%或维持在38.6%可减少52%;降低至95%则增加2.3倍。 - **社交距离情景**:推迟“逐步恢复新常态”(GRNN)政策两个月可稳定流行曲线并缓解病例反弹;在检测到上升趋势后短期内加强社交距离(情景3)可减少32%的累计病例。 **结论与讨论** 研究人员通过反事实情景分析,量化了疫苗部署、检测能力、接触者追踪和社交距离在韩国COVID-19控制中的独立效应。研究结论指出:更早的疫苗部署、持续的检测和接触者追踪能力以及及时的社交距离调整对疫情动态至关重要。在统一建模框架内量化这些效应,为支持大流行防范规划提供了结构化、政策特定的证据。研究强调,检测和接触者追踪作为持续运作的检测型措施,其能力即使小幅下降也与更大的疫情负担相关;疫苗和社交距离的效果则取决于部署或调整的时机。这些发现提示,维持检测能力并谨慎管理依赖时机的干预措施,对未来的大流行应对规划至关重要。研究还指出,反事实情景假设其他条件不变,未考虑行为响应等动态因素,因此估计的效应反映的是政策在理想条件下的独立贡献,实际绝对幅度可能有所不同。未来研究需纳入政策交互和动态行为响应,以优化组合策略。 **研究结果** **前Delta期政策效果评估** 在前Delta期,疫苗覆盖率有限,控制策略主要依赖NPIs。通过情景分析,研究人员发现: - **疫苗接种情景**:提前两个月部署疫苗可使累计确诊病例减少48%(情景4),而延迟两个月则增加14%(情景2)。表明更早部署比更快接种速度影响更大。 - **检测能力情景**:检测能力降至参考水平的97.5%或95%时,病例轨迹在12月高峰后开始上升;降至90%时,病例从3月起快速偏离。 - **接触者追踪情景**:将Q-proportion提高10%或维持在50%可减少约65%的累计确诊病例;而降低至95%则导致病例增加1.9倍。 - **社交距离情景**:在11月病例激增期间加强社交距离强度可有效降低传播,最严格的情景(情景3)使流行曲线明显趋平。 **Delta主导期政策效果评估** Delta时期疫苗快速推进,同时围绕放松社交距离的政策讨论持续。情景分析显示: - **疫苗接种速度情景**:将接种速度提高2.5倍可减少约20%的累计确诊病例并降低Delta暴发峰值;而速度减慢至80%时差异不大。 - **检测能力情景**:若仅检测97.5%的感染,累计病例增加约1.5倍,峰值超过10,000例;若仅检测90%,病例增加4.7倍。 - **接触者追踪情景**:维持Q-proportion在45%可减少74%的病例;提高10%或维持在38.6%可减少52%;降低至95%则增加2.3倍。 - **社交距离情景**:推迟“逐步恢复新常态”(GRNN)政策两个月可稳定流行曲线并缓解病例反弹;在检测到上升趋势后短期内加强社交距离(情景3)可减少32%的累计病例。 **结论与讨论** 研究人员通过反事实情景分析,量化了疫苗部署、检测能力、接触者追踪和社交距离在韩国COVID-19控制中的独立效应。研究结论指出:更早的疫苗部署、持续的检测和接触者追踪能力以及及时的社交距离调整对疫情动态至关重要。在统一建模框架内量化这些效应,为支持大流行防范规划提供了结构化、政策特定的证据。研究强调,检测和接触者追踪作为持续运作的检测型措施,其能力即使小幅下降也与更大的疫情负担相关;疫苗和社交距离的效果则取决于部署或调整的时机。这些发现提示,维持检测能力并谨慎管理依赖时机的干预措施,对未来的大流行应对规划至关重要。研究还指出,反事实情景假设其他条件不变,未考虑行为响应等动态因素,因此估计的效应反映的是政策在理想条件下的独立贡献,实际绝对幅度可能有所不同。未来研究需纳入政策交互和动态行为响应,以优化组合策略。 analysis.event: Counterfactual evaluation of COVID-19 control policies (vaccination, testing, contact tracing, social distancing) using scenario-based modeling. Confirmed research study published in International Journal of Infectious Diseases.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Pre-Delta: Early vaccine deployment reduced cases by 48%; reduced testing or contact tracing increased cases by up to 4.7x. Delta: Delayed relaxation of social distancing reduced rebound; reduced testing increased cases by up to 4.7x. Risk quantified through cumulative case reductions and increases under different scenarios.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Study used calibrated V-SEIQR model with Korean surveillance data. Limitations include assumptions of constant conditions and lack of behavioral response modeling. Findings provide policy-specific evidence for pandemic preparedness planning.

analysis.brief_en: A modeling study published in International Journal of Infectious Diseases evaluated South Korea's COVID-19 control policies through counterfactual scenarios. Analyzing pre-Delta and Delta periods, researchers found that earlier vaccine deployment reduced cases by 48%, while reduced testing or contact tracing significantly increased case burdens. During the Delta wave, delaying relaxation of social distancing measures mitigated rebounds. The study emphasized that maintaining testing capacity and timely adjustments to interventions are critical for pandemic response. The model, calibrated with Korean surveillance data, provided structured evidence for policy planning but noted limitations in assuming static conditions without behavioral responses.
